# WHERE WE GROW NEXT
## An international expansion framework for a European sustainable apparel business
**Board / Executive Committee decision document | v1.0**
**Decision sought: adoption of the *two-track structure*, the beachhead selection method, the gate sequence, and funding of Gate 0. All quantities are calibrated at Gate 0/1 and returned to this Committee for approval.**

---

## The answer in one paragraph

**Stop treating "expand into a new region" as one decision.** Demand entry and supply entry are two different problems with different criteria, different clock speeds, different failure modes and different people running them — and forcing them into the same geography is how mid-sized brands destroy margin in both. Adopt a **two-track model**: a **Demand Track** entering **Japan as a beachhead** (highest willingness-to-pay for material provenance, the lowest apparel return rate of any major market, a wholesale channel that lets us buy market intelligence with someone else's working capital, and a domestic repair-and-resale culture that makes our circularity story native rather than imported), with **South Korea as a fast-follow at Month [30]**; and a **Supply Track** qualifying **Vietnam as primary new-origin manufacturing**, with **India retained for certified organic cotton fibre and fabric** and **Portugal/Turkey retained as nearshore replenishment**. The two tracks are decoupled operationally but joined at exactly one place — the **Origin Bridge (§3.2)**: Vietnam is, we believe, the only new sourcing origin that is duty-advantaged into *both* the EU (EVFTA) and Japan (CPTPP/RCEP/AJCEP), which converts a sourcing decision into a market-access asset instead of a tariff liability. Positioning is *not* "well-made sustainable basics" — Japan already has Uniqlo and Muji and will beat us at that forever (§5). Channels are sequenced credibility-first, capital-last (§6). **One constraint governs everything: the Substantiation Rule (§2.1) — no claim travels faster than its evidence, and no volume travels faster than its audit.**

---

## §0 Scope and status

### 0.1 Status of the numbers

Every share, cost, margin, headcount and threshold in this document is a **design target for calibration, not a measured value**, and is marked *[target]* on first use in each section. They are here because a strategy with no numbers cannot be argued with, and an unarguable strategy cannot be improved. **Gate 0 (§15) replaces them with researched values; Gate 1 replaces those with contracted values.**

Three categories of figure carry different confidence:

| Type | Example | Confidence | Resolved at |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Verifiable fact** | Tariff line, labelling statute, entity threshold | Should be certain — verify, do not estimate | Gate 0, by counsel |
| **Researchable quantity** | Market size, AOV, competitor pricing, CAC benchmark | Estimable to ±[20]% | Gate 0, by field research |
| **Design target** | Our Year-3 revenue, our channel mix, our vendor count | A choice, not a discovery | Gate 1, by this Committee |

The two-track structure (§3); the market-selection criteria and weights (§4); the positioning boundary (§5.2); the channel sequence and its capital discipline (§6); the vendor qualification standard (§9.2); the decision-rights matrix (Appendix B); the gate sequence with its **kill criteria** (§14.4, §15); and €[350–500]k to fund Gate 0.

| In scope | Out of scope (this document) |
|---|---|
| One new demand region, entered via one beachhead country | Wholesale expansion inside existing EU markets |
| One new manufacturing origin, plus fibre sourcing | Renegotiation of existing Portuguese/Turkish vendor terms |

**Rule of the document:** every commitment made to the new market has a stated cost to the core business — management attention, working capital, or inventory risk. Expansion strategies fail in the home market more often than in the target market, and they fail silently.

# WHERE AND HOW WE WORK
## A global operating framework for flexible work
**Executive Committee decision document | v2.0**
**Decision sought: adoption of the *structure* and the decision rights. All quantities are calibrated at Gate 1 and returned to this Committee for approval.**

---

## The answer in one paragraph

**Stop trying to write one work policy for the whole company.** A single global rule — "three days in office," "remote-first," "hybrid" — will be simultaneously too loose for the teams that need co-presence to function and too tight for the teams that don't, and it will be illegal, unaffordable or culturally illegible in a meaningful share of our countries. Instead, adopt a **federated model with three layers**: a thin, non-waivable **Global Spine** (eight commitments that make us one company); a **Country Dial** set by each market against a published dossier of legal, infrastructural and normative constraints; and a **Team Charter** — the real unit of decision — written by every team of roughly 6–15 people and reviewed twice a year. Work is designed against **five work modes and two overlays** (§4), not against days of the week. Offices are re-typed from desk inventory into a **four-format portfolio** whose feasibility depends on one piece of machinery we have never had: **cross-team anchor-day allocation** (§9.2). Roughly [X]% of our workforce cannot choose where they work at all; they are in scope from page one, not as an afterthought (§6). Fairness — proximity bias, geographic pay, apprenticeship — is engineered explicitly (§11), and output measurement is fixed *before* flexibility scales, because otherwise presence quietly becomes the proxy again (§12). **One constraint governs everything: the Subsidiarity Rule (§3) — each decision is made at the lowest layer that can see every person it affects, and no lower.**

---

## §0 Scope and status

### 0.1 Status of the numbers

Every ratio, day-count, square-metre figure, stipend value and threshold in this document is a **design target for calibration, not a measured value**, and is marked *[target]* on first use in each section. They are included because a framework with no numbers cannot be argued with, and an unarguable framework cannot be improved. **Gate 1 (§16) replaces them with measured values**; the Committee approves the calibrated set before any policy is communicated to employees.

What we are asking the Committee to adopt today is: the three-layer structure, the eight Spine commitments, the five modes, the four office formats, the decision-rights matrix (Appendix C), the gate sequence, and the funding of Gate 1.

### 0.2 Who this covers

The phrase "future of work" has been used inside the company as a synonym for "hybrid office work." That framing excludes a large minority — possibly a majority — of our people, and it is the fastest route to a two-class company.

| Population | Illustrative share *[target — Gate 1 to measure]* | What flexibility means here | Governed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **A. Location-flexible** | ~[40]% | Where and when, within team and country limits | §§3–5, 7–12 |
| **B. Fixed-location** — manufacturing, warehouse, retail, lab, clinical, site security, catering, field maintenance | ~[45]% | **When**, not where: schedule predictability, shift choice, roster self-scheduling, compressed weeks, time-in-lieu, leave access | §6 (parallel framework, equal status) |
| **C. Mixed** — field service, sales, engineers with lab or site dependencies, plant supervisors | ~[15]% | Site-anchored days plus flexible remainder; the *anchor* is set by the site, the remainder by the Charter | §6.3 |

**Rule of the document:** wherever this framework grants something to population A, §6 states the equivalent grant to B and C, or explains why no equivalent exists. Wherever we report a fairness metric (§11.4), all three populations appear in the cut. A benefit that only knowledge workers can consume is not a benefit; it is a differential.

---

## §1 Stating the problem correctly

The debate has been framed as *remote vs. office*. That axis is unhelpful, because it treats location as the variable when location is a **consequence**.

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| How many days in the office? | What work do we do that is *degraded* by distance, and how much of it is there? |
| Is remote work productive? | Which roles have output that is legible without co-presence — and which have we simply never learned to measure? (§12) |
| How do we get people back? | What must the office be *good at* that a home desk isn't, and are our buildings currently good at it? |
| What's our policy? | Who decides, at what layer, with what evidence, and who hears the appeal? (§3, §15) |

**Corollary 1.** Attendance is not a goal. It is an input we may or may not need. A policy expressed *purely* as a day-count is a confession that the analysis wasn't done. (Day-count *bands* have exactly one legitimate use — real-estate planning and legal negotiation. That use is fenced in §7.3.)

**Corollary 2.** Most of the pain reported as "hybrid isn't working" is not about location. It is about **meeting load, unclear decision rights, documentation debt, time-zone tax and untrained managers**. Those are fixable independent of where anyone sits; they are cheaper than real estate; and they compound. **Sequence them first** (§16, Gate 2 wave 1).

---

## §2 What we are optimising for

Named explicitly, because unnamed objectives get traded away silently.

**A gate, not a priority:** *Legal, tax and collective-agreement integrity.* No arrangement that creates permanent-establishment exposure, misclassifies employment, breaches a works-council agreement or violates working-time law. This is not ranked against anything; it is a pass/fail test applied before options are compared. Legal and Tax hold a veto, not an opinion.

**The five ranked objectives**, in priority order when they conflict:

| Rank | Objective | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Equity of opportunity** | A person's promotion odds are not predicted by their distance from a headquarters, their work pattern, or their population (A/B/C) |
| **2** | **Output quality and speed** | Team-level delivery against commitments, measured per §12 |
| **3** | **Cohesion** | Enough shared context that the company can change direction without fracturing |
| **4** | **Talent access** | Hiring and retention in labour markets a full-return policy would close to us |
| **5** | **Cost discipline** | Real estate and workplace spend per employee, against the §14 bridge |

Equity outranks output because equity failures are slow, compounding and legally actionable, while output problems are visible and correctable. Cost is last because savings taken out of cohesion and equity are borrowed, not earned.

### 2.1 Adjudication — who breaks the tie

An unarbitrated priority list is decorative. Therefore:

- Conflicts between objectives are decided by the **Work Design Council** (§15.1) on a written submission that names the objectives in tension, the evidence, and the population affected.
- **Burden of proof sits with the lower-ranked objective.** A cost proposal that reduces equity or cohesion must quantify the saving *and* the harm, and propose mitigation. "It's cheaper" is not an argument; it is a number awaiting an argument.
- Any decision that overrides objective 1 requires **CPO + CEO** sign-off and is entered in the Exception Register (§15.3) with a review date.
- The Council publishes its decisions internally. Precedent is how a federated model stays coherent without a rulebook.

---

## §3 The Subsidiarity Rule and the three layers

> **Subsidiarity Rule:** Every decision about where and how work happens is made at the lowest layer that can see every person it affects — and no lower.

A decision affecting one team's week belongs to that team. A decision affecting statutory rights belongs to the country. A decision affecting whether two teams on different continents can ship together belongs to the centre. Pushing a decision *up* costs speed and fit; pushing it *down* costs coherence and manufactures local unfairness.

| Layer | Owner | Scope | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Global Spine** | Executive Committee | 8 commitments. Universal, non-waivable. | Annual review |
| **Country Dial** | Country lead + HR + Legal, with works council where applicable | Legal floor, stipend values, office footprint and format mix, planning band, local core hours, right-to-disconnect implementation, language of record | Semi-annual |
| **Team Charter** | Team lead with the team | Mode profile, together-time and its purpose, core overlap, response-time norms, meeting inventory, decision protocol, onboarding, inclusion check | Semi-annual, published |

Full decision rights, including who may *not* decide what, are in **Appendix C**.

### 3.1 The Global Spine (adopt or amend; do not expand)

**S1 — Purpose before place.** Every requirement to be somewhere must name the work mode (§4) it serves. "Because it's Tuesday" is not a reason.

**S2 — Every team has a written, published Charter.** Unwritten norms are how proximity bias enters a company. If it isn't written, it isn't a norm; it's a hazard.

**S3 — Written-first for decisions, specs and context.** These live in a durable, searchable, permissioned place. *Scope limit:* S3 governs **decisions, specifications and context only**. It explicitly does **not** apply to 1:1s, coaching, sensitive feedback, performance conversations, wellbeing discussions or relationship time — documenting those would be both chilling and, in several jurisdictions, unlawful. The old formulation ("a meeting with no artefact did not happen") is withdrawn as absolutist; the replacement test is: *if a decision was made and is not written down, it will be re-made.*

**S4 — Meetings are opt-in for information, opt-out for decisions.** No standing meeting survives two quarters without explicit renewal by its owner in the Charter's meeting inventory.

**S5 — One time-zone tax, shared.** Recurring cross-region meetings rotate their inconvenience; no region is permanently the one dialling in at 22:00.
*Exception path (mandatory, because rotation is sometimes impossible):* where the counterparty is a customer, a market open, a regulator or a plant shift, a **Standing Unsociable-Hours Exception** may be granted by the regional leader for ≤12 months, renewable, entered in the Exception Register, and only with one of four compensating remedies named: (a) follow-the-sun redesign so the handoff replaces the meeting; (b) hiring or relocating for overlap; (c) time-in-lieu at a published rate; (d) an unsociable-hours allowance where local law and practice support it. An exception with no remedy is refused.

**S6 — Same job, same access.** Location and work pattern do not change eligibility for projects, promotion, sponsorship, budget or information. Where location changes *compensation*, the rule is published, zone-based and applied mechanically (§11.2).

**S7 — A baseline environment guarantee, for everyone.** Every employee has a safe, connected, ergonomically adequate place to work — at home, in a company office, at a paid third space, or **at their site**, at company cost, at levels set by the Country Dial. For population B this reads as facilities standards: rest space, lockers, connectivity, decent break areas, and equivalent per-head workplace spend. Population B must not fund population A's stipends out of its own neglected estate.

**S8 — Nothing that breaks local law, tax status or a collective agreement.** No exceptions, no goodwill workarounds, no "just for this one hire."

Eight is the ceiling. Every additional global rule must be true simultaneously in Lagos, Stuttgart, Bengaluru, São Paulo, Osaka and Salt Lake City — and very few things are.

---

## §4 The five work modes and two overlays

Modes, not days, are the design unit. Sort a team's actual month into these five, apply the overlays, and its Charter largely writes itself.

### 4.1 The five modes (mutually exclusive; every hour lands in exactly one)

| # | Mode | Discriminating test | Distance sensitivity | Best setting | Primary enabler |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **M1** | **Deep focus** | One person producing; interruption is the enemy | **Negative** — co-presence usually *harms* it | **Any environment the individual controls and can reach reliably** — home study, quiet office zone, or a Touchdown site (§9.1) where home is not viable | Calendar protection; do-not-disturb norms |
| **M2** | **Convergent work** | *Someone has to change their mind or merge two positions.* Known problem, needs a decision | Low–moderate | Anywhere with good tooling; short sync after async pre-read | Pre-read + 30-min call + written decision |
| **M3** | **Divergent work** | *Nobody knows the answer yet.* Ambiguity, generation, productive conflict, whiteboarding | **High** | Same room, writable walls, 2–6 hour blocks | In-person workshop; digital canvas as an honest second-best |
| **M4** | **Apprenticeship and tacit transfer** | *Someone is learning judgement that isn't written down.* | **Very high** | Same room, sustained, with unscheduled overhearing | Co-location blocks; work-alongs; senior time budget (§11.3) |
| **M5** | **Coordination and handoff** | *Someone needs to know something at the right time.* Status, dependencies, handoffs | Low, **if disciplined** | Nowhere in particular | Written status; overlap window; single source of truth |

M2 vs M5 is the distinction teams get wrong. **Changing a mind is M2. Transferring knowledge is M5.** If a recurring meeting only transmits information, it is M5 and should be a document.

### 4.2 The two overlays (not modes — do not allocate percentages to them)

- **Overlay T — Trust formation.** Relational credit is an *investment* that makes M2 and M3 cheap, not a mode of work. It is therefore handled as a **named budget and cadence** — offsites, shared meals, travel — owned at the Charter level and funded per §14.3. Design target *[target]*: every distributed team is physically together **at least twice a year**, and no employee goes **more than six months** without being in a room with colleagues. Treating trust as a byproduct is how distributed teams die quietly.
- **Overlay C — Customer, site and shift override.** For customer-facing, field and site-dependent work, location is determined by the customer or the asset, not by us. Overlay C **overrides** the mode's preferred setting for the hours it applies to; the underlying mode is still recorded (a salesperson doing discovery in a client's boardroom is doing M3 under Overlay C). This eliminates the double-counting that a "customer-facing mode" would have guaranteed.

## §1 Stating the problem correctly

The debate has been framed as *remote vs. office*. That axis is unhelpful, because it treats location as the variable when location is a **consequence**.

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| How many days in the office? | What work do we do that is *degraded* by distance, and how much of it is there? |
| Is remote work productive? | Which roles have output that is legible without co-presence — and which have we simply never learned to measure? (§12) |
| How do we get people back? | What must the office be *good at* that a home desk isn't, and are our buildings currently good at it? |
| What's our policy? | Who decides, at what layer, with what evidence, and who hears the appeal? (§3, §15) |

**Corollary 1.** Attendance is not a goal. It is an input we may or may not need. A policy expressed *purely* as a day-count is a confession that the analysis wasn't done. (Day-count *bands* have exactly one legitimate use — real-estate planning and legal negotiation. That use is fenced in §7.3.)

**Corollary 2.** Most of the pain reported as "hybrid isn't working" is not about location. It is about **meeting load, unclear decision rights, documentation debt, time-zone tax and untrained managers**. Named explicitly, because unnamed objectives get traded away silently.

**The five ranked objectives**, in priority order when they conflict:

| Rank | Objective | Test |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **Equity of opportunity** | A person's promotion odds are not predicted by their distance from a headquarters, their work pattern, or their population (A/B/C) |
| **2** | **Output quality and speed** | Team-level delivery against commitments, measured per §12 |
| **3** | **Cohesion** | Enough shared context that the company can change direction without fracturing |
| **4** | **Talent access** | Hiring and retention in labour markets a full-return policy would close to us |
| **5** | **Cost discipline** | Real estate and workplace spend per employee, against the §14 bridge |

An unarbitrated priority list is decorative. Therefore:

- Conflicts between objectives are decided by the **Work Design Council** (§15.1) on a written submission that names the objectives in tension, the evidence, and the population affected.
- **Burden of proof sits with the lower-ranked objective.** A cost proposal that reduces equity or cohesion must quantify the saving *and* the harm, and propose mitigation. "It's cheaper" is not an argument; it is a number awaiting an argument.
- Any decision that overrides objective 1 requires **CPO + CEO** sign-off and is entered in the Exception Register (§15.3) with a review date.
- The Council publishes its decisions internally. Precedent is how a federated model stays coherent without a rulebook.

## §3 The Subsidiarity Rule and the three layers

> **Subsidiarity Rule:** Every decision about where and how work happens is made at the lowest layer that can see every person it affects — and no lower.

A decision affecting one team's week belongs to that team. A decision affecting statutory rights belongs to the country. A decision affecting whether two teams on different continents can ship together belongs to the centre. Pushing a decision *up* costs speed and fit; pushing it *down* costs coherence and manufactures local unfairness.

| Layer | Owner | Scope | Cadence |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Global Spine** | Executive Committee | 8 commitments. Universal, non-waivable. | Annual review |
| **Country Dial** | Country lead + HR + Legal, with works council where applicable | Legal floor, stipend values, office footprint and format mix, planning band, local core hours, right-to-disconnect implementation, language of record | Semi-annual |
| **Team Charter** | Team lead with the team | Mode profile, together-time and its purpose, core overlap, response-time norms, meeting inventory, decision protocol, onboarding, inclusion check | Semi-annual, published |

Full decision rights, including who may *not* decide what, are in **Appendix C**.

### 3.1 The Global Spine (adopt or amend; do not expand)

**S1 — Purpose before place.** Every requirement to be somewhere must name the work mode (§4) it serves. "Because it's Tuesday" is not a reason.

**S2 — Every team has a written, published Charter.** Unwritten norms are how proximity bias enters a company. If it isn't written, it isn't a norm; it's a hazard.

**S3 — Written-first for decisions, specs and context.** These live in a durable, searchable, permissioned place. *Scope limit:* S3 governs **decisions, specifications and context only**. It explicitly does **not** apply to 1:1s, coaching, sensitive feedback, performance conversations, wellbeing discussions or relationship time — documenting those would be both chilling and, in several jurisdictions, unlawful. The old formulation ("a meeting with no artefact did not happen") is withdrawn as absolutist; the replacement test is: *if a decision was made and is not written down, it will be re-made.*

**S4 — Meetings are opt-in for information, opt-out for decisions.** No standing meeting survives two quarters without explicit renewal by its owner in the Charter's meeting inventory.

**S5 — One time-zone tax, shared.** Recurring cross-region meetings rotate their inconvenience; no region is permanently the one dialling in at 22:00.
*Exception path (mandatory, because rotation is sometimes impossible):* where the counterparty is a customer, a market open, a regulator or a plant shift, a **Standing Unsociable-Hours Exception** may be granted by the regional leader for ≤12 months, renewable, entered in the Exception Register, and only with one of four compensating remedies named: (a) follow-the-sun redesign so the handoff replaces the meeting; (b) hiring or relocating for overlap; (c) time-in-lieu at a published rate; (d) an unsociable-hours allowance where local law and practice support it. **S6 — Same job, same access.** Location and work pattern do not change eligibility for projects, promotion, sponsorship, budget or information. Where location changes *compensation*, the rule is published, zone-based and applied mechanically (§11.2).

**S8 — Nothing that breaks local law, tax status or a collective agreement.** No exceptions, no goodwill workarounds, no "just for this one hire."

| Type | Example | Confidence | Resolved at |
|---|---|---|---|

| **Researchable quantity** | Market size, AOV, competitor pricing, CAC benchmark | Estimable to ±[20]% | Gate 0, by field research |

### 0.2 What we are asking the Committee to adopt today

### 0.3 Who and what this covers

| In scope | Out of scope (this document) |

| One new demand region, entered via one beachhead country | Wholesale expansion inside existing EU markets |
| One new manufacturing origin, plus fibre sourcing | Renegotiation of existing Portuguese/Turkish vendor terms |

**Rule of the document:** every commitment made to the new market has a stated cost to the core business — management attention, working capital, or inventory risk. Expansion strategies fail in the home market more often than in the target market, and they fail silently.

| Wrong question | Right question |

| Which country next? | What are we short of — customers, margin, capacity, or credibility — and which geography is the cheapest source of *that specific thing*? |
| Where can we sell sustainable clothing? | Where is sustainability a **purchase driver** rather than a **tiebreaker**, and where is it neither? |

---

## 2. Structural pastiche from the prior document

The framework is transplanted from the flexible-work document almost node for node: "The answer in one paragraph," "§0 Scope and status," "0.1 Status of the numbers," "Every ratio... is a design target for calibration, not a measured value," "§1 Stating the problem correctly," the Wrong question/Right question table, "Corollary 1 / Corollary 2," "**One constraint governs everything: the X Rule**," the gate sequence, the decision-rights appendix.

Two consequences:

- **Proportionality failure.** The prior document governed a global workforce across dozens of jurisdictions; that justified councils, exception registers, and layered decision rights. This is a *mid-sized* apparel company. A board-grade gate apparatus, a decision-rights matrix, a calibration taxonomy, and a €350–500k pre-strategy research spend may exceed what the organisation can metabolise. The document itself argues (correctly, and it is the best line in the piece) that expansion fails at home through drained management attention — and then proposes an attention-intensive governance overlay without ever costing that irony.
- **Genre drift.** Governance scaffolding is substituting for market knowledge. The reader learns a great deal about how decisions will be staged and almost nothing about Japan.

**Fix:** cut the meta-apparatus by half. Keep the three-tier confidence table (genuinely useful) and the kill criteria. Drop the appendix-level decision-rights machinery to a half-page.

---

## 3. The Origin Bridge contains a probable internal contradiction

This is the sharpest technical problem. The summary makes Vietnam's dual duty preference — EVFTA into the EU, CPTPP/RCEP/AJCEP into Japan — the single hinge joining both tracks. Simultaneously, it states that **India is retained for certified organic cotton fibre and fabric**.

Apparel preference regimes are governed by rules of origin, not by the location of the sewing line. EVFTA's textile rules are broadly **fabric-forward** with limited cumulation (EU, Korea); CPTPP textile rules are broadly **yarn-forward**. If Indian fabric is cut and sewn in Vietnam, the resulting garment may **fail** origin under one or both regimes and attract full MFN duty — precisely the "tariff liability" the Bridge claims to convert into an asset. The document does not flag this. It is the one thing a sourcing-literate reader will check first, and it is currently unaddressed.

Two further issues in the same claim:

- **"Vietnam is... the only new sourcing origin duty-advantaged into both the EU and Japan"** is overstated. Cambodia is a plausible counterexample (EU Everything But Arms plus RCEP/AJCEP/Japanese GSP treatment), and Vietnam's uniqueness on the EU side depends on which comparators are treated as "new." The hedge ("we believe," Gate 0 verification) is appropriate in principle, but the claim is load-bearing for the entire two-track thesis and is presented in the executive summary as the reason the strategy holds together. A load-bearing claim should not be a "we believe."
- **Preference erosion risk is acknowledged generically** ("regimes graduate, expire and change") but not applied: EVFTA tariff phase-downs, Vietnamese wage inflation, and possible EU CBAM/CSDDD-adjacent compliance cost are all live and none appear as a sensitivity.

---

## 4. Japan is asserted, not derived

The summary names Japan as beachhead before §4 (selection criteria and weights) has been written. Because §4 is missing, the reader cannot test whether the stated criteria actually select Japan — the classic reasoning-in-reverse pattern that the document's own §1 framing warns against.

Substantively, several of the Japan claims are contestable and are presented in the argument slot rather than the research slot:

- **"Highest willingness-to-pay for material provenance."** Japanese consumers show high *craft and quality* literacy; cross-market surveys generally do **not** place Japan at the top for sustainability-as-purchase-driver, and Japan is a structurally price-deflationary apparel market. The document's own right-question — "where is sustainability a purchase driver rather than a tiebreaker" — arguably points away from Japan and toward Northern Europe, North America, or Korea.
- **"Lowest apparel return rate of any major market"** is stated as fact with no source. If true it is a real margin advantage worth quantifying; as written it is an unfootnoted assertion in a document that elsewhere insists on evidence discipline.
- **Japan's difficulty for mid-sized foreign brands is not priced.** Long relationship cycles with select-shop buyers, exacting service and packaging expectations, Japanese-language support as table stakes, sizing and size-curve differences, distributor dependence, high cost of a physical presence. Japan is a high-credibility, high-cost, slow-payback market — defensible, but only if the cost of patience is stated.
- **No counterfactual is dismissed.** For a Western European sustainable brand, North America is the obvious alternative (largest premium sustainable segment, English-language, DTC-native, faster feedback loops), and Australia offers counter-seasonal inventory clearance — a genuinely valuable structural benefit for an apparel business that the document never mentions. At minimum, a shortlist table with three to five candidates, the weights, and one-line rejections is required.
- **South Korea "fast-follow at Month [30]"** is unjustified. Korea is arguably the faster, cheaper, more digital-native entry and could plausibly lead. The sequencing needs an argument, not a bracket.

---

## 5. The two-track decoupling is weaker than claimed

"The two tracks are decoupled operationally but joined at exactly one place" is contradicted two sections later by Corollary 2, which identifies management attention and working capital as the dominant failure mode. That is a second, third and fourth coupling: executive bandwidth, cash, and the fact that a new manufacturing origin changes the cost base of the *home* market and therefore its pricing and inventory decisions.

Also missing: **the sequencing option is never considered.** Three viable shapes exist —
(a) supply first, harvest margin, fund demand entry from it;
(b) demand first, prove volume, then justify capacity;
(c) simultaneous.
The document silently chooses (c), the most attention-expensive option, for the company type least able to afford it. An explicit attention budget ("this consumes X% of the CEO/COO/CPO year, funded by dropping Y") would resolve both this and the proportionality problem in §2 above.

Finally, the Origin Bridge creates a **dependency risk** that is not named: if Vietnam qualification slips, the Japan margin thesis degrades with it — the opposite of decoupling.

---

## 6. Content gaps that a mid-sized apparel entrant cannot afford

Even allowing for truncation, none of the following appears in the delivered sections or in the roadmap of section titles, and several are Gate 0 items rather than later-stage detail:

- **Trademark clearance in Nice Class 25 in Japan/Korea, plus kana/katakana brand transliteration and domain/handle availability.** Squatting and prior registration have killed entries outright. This belongs on page one of operational steps, not implied.
- **Entity and importer-of-record decision:** KK vs GK vs no entity (distributor as IOR), consumption-tax/JCT registration, transfer-pricing implications.
- **Japan-specific labelling and consumer law:** Household Goods Quality Labelling Act (fibre composition and care labelling in Japanese), Act on Specified Commercial Transactions disclosures for e-commerce, Consumer Affairs Agency greenwashing guidance. The Substantiation Rule is a good instinct but is never connected to a single named regime — including the EU ones the company already lives under (Empowering Consumers / Green Claims, ESPR digital product passport for textiles, CSRD/CSDDD).
- **Positioning content.** The document says what the positioning is *not* (Uniqlo/Muji territory) and stops. Naming the enemy is not a proposition. State affirmatively what the brand is for in Japan, the price architecture and psychological price points, the SKU and size-curve adaptation, the seasonal calendar, and — critically — **why a Beams or United Arrows buyer would take an unknown European brand at all.** The wholesale-as-cheap-market-intelligence argument is excellent, but it assumes access it has not earned.
- **Channel specifics.** LINE rather than the Western messaging default; Rakuten vs Zozotown vs Amazon JP vs own DTC; konbini/COD payment expectations; PR-led launch and Japanese KOL norms; pop-up geography (Daikanyama, Parco). The phrase "credibility-first, capital-last" is a good principle awaiting content.
- **Financials.** No indicative envelope, no revenue/margin shape, no payback period, no break-even volume. A board asked to fund Gate 0 will ask what Gate 0 is a gate *to*. Withholding the envelope is defensible; withholding an order of magnitude is not.
- **Risk register and exit.** Kill criteria are promised at §14.4/§15 but the concept of a reversible entry (distributor-first, so exit costs a contract rather than a lease and a payroll) is never made explicit — even though it is the natural conclusion of the document's own capital discipline.

---

## 7. Smaller errors and inconsistencies

- **"€[350–500]k"** — a 43% spread is not a fundable ask. Give a number with a contingency line.
- **"Estimable to ±[20]%"** — a blanket precision claim applied to niche premium segment sizing in a foreign market. It will not be ±20%. Either differentiate by item or drop the figure.
- **Audience confusion:** the header addresses "Board / Executive Committee." These want different documents and can approve different things (a board with outside investors changes what may be asked). Pick one.
- **"Month [30]"** for Korea is spuriously precise relative to everything around it; use a trigger condition ("Korea entry opens when Japan hits [X] repeat rate and [Y] wholesale doors"), which is also more consistent with the gate philosophy.

- **Wrong-question table:** five rows with overlap between rows 1 and 3 (both are cost/consequence framings). Three sharper rows beat five.
- **Stylistic saturation:** three aphorisms of identical construction ("no claim travels faster than its evidence," "cannot be argued with... cannot be improved," "or they are guesses") in under two pages. The register begins to read as house style rather than analysis, which undercuts the empiricism being claimed.

---

- **Separating demand entry from supply entry** is the correct central insight and is the document's real contribution. Most treatments of this brief conflate them.
- **Corollary 1 (landed-cost-after-risk)** is precise, correctly ordered, and immediately usable.
- **Corollary 2 ("most international expansion failure is domestic")** is the single most valuable sentence here — and should be promoted into a hard constraint with an attention budget attached, not left as an aphorism.
- **The three-tier confidence taxonomy** (verifiable fact / researchable quantity / design target) is a genuinely strong governance device and better than the single "[target]" convention it inherited.
- **Wholesale-first as buying market truth with someone else's working capital** is exactly right for a mid-sized brand's capital position.
- **"Rule of the document: every commitment has a stated cost to the core"** is a good discipline

Three categories of figure carry different confidence:

| Type | Example | Confidence | Resolved at |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Verifiable fact** | Tariff line, labelling statute, entity threshold | Should be certain — verify, do not estimate | Gate 0, by counsel |
| **Researchable quantity** | Market size, AOV, competitor pricing, CAC benchmark | Estimable to ±[20]% | Gate 0, by field research |
| **Design target** | Our Year-3 revenue, our channel mix, our vendor count | A choice, not a discovery | Gate 1, by this Committee |

**Anything in this document touching tariff preference, rules of origin, GSP eligibility or labelling law is a Gate 0 verification item, not a settled fact.** Trade preference regimes graduate, expire and change; a strategy built on a lapsed preference is a strategy built on nothing.

### 0.2 What we are asking the Committee to adopt today

The two-track structure (§3); the market-selection criteria and weights (§4); the positioning boundary (§5.2); the channel sequence and its capital discipline (§6); the vendor qualification standard (§9.2); the decision-rights matrix (Appendix B); the gate sequence with its **kill criteria** (§14.4, §15); and €[350–500]k to fund Gate 0.

We are **not** asking for approval of the full investment envelope, the beachhead country as an irrevocable choice, or any hiring beyond the Gate 0 team.

### 0.3 Who and what this covers

| In scope | Out of scope (this document) |
|---|---|
| One new demand region, entered via one beachhead country | Wholesale expansion inside existing EU markets |
| One new manufacturing origin, plus fibre sourcing | Renegotiation of existing Portuguese/Turkish vendor terms |
| The organisational capacity to run both without degrading the core | M&A, licensing-out, franchising |
| Sustainability substantiation infrastructure (which we need anyway) | Product architecture redesign beyond market-fit adaptation |

**Rule of the document:** every commitment made to the new market has a stated cost to the core business — management attention, working capital, or inventory risk. Expansion strategies fail in the home market more often than in the target market, and they fail silently.

---

## §1 Stating the problem correctly

The question has been framed as *"which country next?"* That is the wrong axis, because country is a **consequence** of what we are trying to buy.

| Wrong question | Right question |
|---|---|
| Which country next? | What are we short of — customers, margin, capacity, or credibility — and which geography is the cheapest source of *that specific thing*? |
| Where can we sell sustainable clothing? | Where is sustainability a **purchase driver** rather than a **tiebreaker**, and where is it neither? |
| Where can we manufacture more cheaply? | What is our **landed cost after duty, freight, defect rate, lead-time inventory and audit overhead** — and is it actually lower? |
| Should we go DTC or wholesale? | What is the cheapest way to buy market truth before we commit capital that cannot be recovered? |
| How do we translate our brand? | Which of our claims survive contact with a market that has better craft literacy than our home market? |

**Corollary 1 — Cheap labour is not cheap.** FOB price is the smallest and least reliable term in the landed-cost equation. A [15]% FOB saving is erased by an [11]% duty, a [4]-week lead-time extension financed as inventory, a [2]-point defect rate, or one supply-chain labour finding that costs us a retail listing. Sourcing decisions are **landed-cost-after-risk** decisions or they are guesses.

**Corollary 2 — Most "international expansion failure" is domestic.** It is under-resourced management attention, working cap

# CRITIQUE: "Where We Grow Next" (v1.0)

## 1. The disqualifying problem: the document does not exist yet

The output terminates mid-word ("working cap") at §1, Corollary 2. What has been delivered is a cover page, a scope section, a numbers-status section, and a problem-framing table — roughly §0–§1 of a document that forward-references §§2–15 plus Appendices A and B.

The original request asked for three specific things:

| Requested | Delivered |
|---|---|
| Product positioning | A negation ("not well-made sustainable basics"), plus a forward reference to §5 |
| Marketing channels | The phrase "sequenced credibility-first, capital-last," plus a forward reference to §6 |
| Initial operational steps | A €[350–500]k Gate 0 ask, plus forward references to §9.2, §14.4, §15 |

All three requested deliverables are promissory. The summary paragraph is doing the work that the body was supposed to do, which means the reader gets conclusions with no exposed reasoning. This is not a matter of polish; roughly 85% of the substance is missing.

---

## 2. Structural pastiche from the prior document

The framework is transplanted from the flexible-work document almost node for node: "The answer in one paragraph," "§0 Scope and status," "0.1 Status of the numbers," "Every ratio... is a design target for calibration, not a measured value," "§1 Stating the problem correctly," the Wrong question/Right question table, "Corollary 1 / Corollary 2," "**One constraint governs everything: the X Rule**," the gate sequence, the decision-rights appendix.

Two consequences:

- **Proportionality failure.** The prior document governed a global workforce across dozens of jurisdictions; that justified councils, exception registers, and layered decision rights. This is a *mid-sized* apparel company. A board-grade gate apparatus, a decision-rights matrix, a calibration taxonomy, and a €350–500k pre-strategy research spend may exceed what the organisation can metabolise. The document itself argues (correctly, and it is the best line in the piece) that expansion fails at home through drained management attention — and then proposes an attention-intensive governance overlay without ever costing that irony.
- **Genre drift.** Governance scaffolding is substituting for market knowledge. The reader learns a great deal about how decisions will be staged and almost nothing about Japan.

**Fix:** cut the meta-apparatus by half. Keep the three-tier confidence table (genuinely useful) and the kill criteria. Drop the appendix-level decision-rights machinery to a half-page.

---

## 3. The Origin Bridge contains a probable internal contradiction

This is the sharpest technical problem. The summary makes Vietnam's dual duty preference — EVFTA into the EU, CPTPP/RCEP/AJCEP into Japan — the single hinge joining both tracks. Simultaneously, it states that **India is retained for certified organic cotton fibre and fabric**.

Apparel preference regimes are governed by rules of origin, not by the location of the sewing line. EVFTA's textile rules are broadly **fabric-forward** with limited cumulation (EU, Korea); CPTPP textile rules are broadly **yarn-forward**. If Indian fabric is cut and sewn in Vietnam, the resulting garment may **fail** origin under one or both regimes and attract full MFN duty — precisely the "tariff liability" the Bridge claims to convert into an asset. The document does not flag this. It is the one thing a sourcing-literate reader will check first, and it is currently unaddressed.

Two further issues in the same claim:

- **"Vietnam is... the only new sourcing origin duty-advantaged into both the EU and Japan"** is overstated. Cambodia is a plausible counterexample (EU Everything But Arms plus RCEP/AJCEP/Japanese GSP treatment), and Vietnam's uniqueness on the EU side depends on which comparators are treated as "new." The hedge ("we believe," Gate 0 verification) is appropriate in principle, but the claim is load-bearing for the entire two-track thesis and is presented in the executive summary as the reason the strategy holds together. A load-bearing claim should not be a "we believe."
- **Preference erosion risk is acknowledged generically** ("regimes graduate, expire and change") but not applied: EVFTA tariff phase-downs, Vietnamese wage inflation, and possible EU CBAM/CSDDD-adjacent compliance cost are all live and none appear as a sensitivity.

---

## 4. Japan is asserted, not derived

The summary names Japan as beachhead before §4 (selection criteria and weights) has been written. Because §4 is missing, the reader cannot test whether the stated criteria actually select Japan — the classic reasoning-in-reverse pattern that the document's own §1 framing warns against.

Substantively, several of the Japan claims are contestable and are presented in the argument slot rather than the research slot:

- **"Highest willingness-to-pay for material provenance."** Japanese consumers show high *craft and quality* literacy; cross-market surveys generally do **not** place Japan at the top for sustainability-as-purchase-driver, and Japan is a structurally price-deflationary apparel market. The document's own right-question — "where is sustainability a purchase driver rather than a tiebreaker" — arguably points away from Japan and toward Northern Europe, North America, or Korea.
- **"Lowest apparel return rate of any major market"** is stated as fact with no source. If true it is a real margin advantage worth quantifying; as written it is an unfootnoted assertion in a document that elsewhere insists on evidence discipline.
- **Japan's difficulty for mid-sized foreign brands is not priced.** Long relationship cycles with select-shop buyers, exacting service and packaging expectations, Japanese-language support as table stakes, sizing and size-curve differences, distributor dependence, high cost of a physical presence. Japan is a high-credibility, high-cost, slow-payback market — defensible, but only if the cost of patience is stated.
- **No counterfactual is dismissed.** For a Western European sustainable brand, North America is the obvious alternative (largest premium sustainable segment, English-language, DTC-native, faster feedback loops), and Australia offers counter-seasonal inventory clearance — a genuinely valuable structural benefit for an apparel business that the document never mentions. At minimum, a shortlist table with three to five candidates, the weights, and one-line rejections is required.
- **South Korea "fast-follow at Month [30]"** is unjustified. Korea is arguably the faster, cheaper, more digital-native entry and could plausibly lead. The sequencing needs an argument, not a bracket.

---

## 5. The two-track decoupling is weaker than claimed

"The two tracks are decoupled operationally but joined at exactly one place" is contradicted two sections later by Corollary 2, which identifies management attention and working capital as the dominant failure mode. That is a second, third and fourth coupling: executive bandwidth, cash, and the fact that a new manufacturing origin changes the cost base of the *home* market and therefore its pricing and inventory decisions.

Also missing: **the sequencing option is never considered.** Three viable shapes exist —
(a) supply first, harvest margin, fund demand entry from it;
(b) demand first, prove volume, then justify capacity;
(c) simultaneous.
The document silently chooses (c), the most attention-expensive option, for the company type least able to afford it. An explicit attention budget ("this consumes X% of the CEO/COO/CPO year, funded by dropping Y") would resolve both this and the proportionality problem in §2 above.

Finally, the Origin Bridge creates a **dependency risk** that is not named: if Vietnam qualification slips, the Japan margin thesis degrades with it — the opposite of decoupling.

---

## 6. Content gaps that a mid-sized apparel entrant cannot afford

Even allowing for truncation, none of the following appears in the delivered sections or in the roadmap of section titles, and several are Gate 0 items rather than later-stage detail:

- **Trademark clearance in Nice Class 25 in Japan/Korea, plus kana/katakana brand transliteration and domain/handle availability.** Squatting and prior registration have killed entries outright. This belongs on page one of operational steps, not implied.
- **Entity and importer-of-record decision:** KK vs GK vs no entity (distributor as IOR), consumption-tax/JCT registration, transfer-pricing implications.
- **Japan-specific labelling and consumer law:** Household Goods Quality Labelling Act (fibre composition and care labelling in Japanese), Act on Specified Commercial Transactions disclosures for e-commerce, Consumer Affairs Agency greenwashing guidance. The Substantiation Rule is a good instinct but is never connected to a single named regime — including the EU ones the company already lives under (Empowering Consumers / Green Claims, ESPR digital product passport for textiles, CSRD/CSDDD).
- **Positioning content.** The document says what the positioning is *not* (Uniqlo/Muji territory) and stops. Naming the enemy is not a proposition. State affirmatively what the brand is for in Japan, the price architecture and psychological price points, the SKU and size-curve adaptation, the seasonal calendar, and — critically — **why a Beams or United Arrows buyer would take an unknown European brand at all.** The wholesale-as-cheap-market-intelligence argument is excellent, but it assumes access it has not earned.
- **Channel specifics.** LINE rather than the Western messaging default; Rakuten vs Zozotown vs Amazon JP vs own DTC; konbini/COD payment expectations; PR-led launch and Japanese KOL norms; pop-up geography (Daikanyama, Parco). The phrase "credibility-first, capital-last" is a good principle awaiting content.
- **Financials.** No indicative envelope, no revenue/margin shape, no payback period, no break-even volume. A board asked to fund Gate 0 will ask what Gate 0 is a gate *to*. Withholding the envelope is defensible; withholding an order of magnitude is not.
- **Risk register and exit.** Kill criteria are promised at §14.4/§15 but the concept of a reversible entry (distributor-first, so exit costs a contract rather than a lease and a payroll) is never made explicit — even though it is the natural conclusion of the document's own capital discipline.

---

## 7. Smaller errors and inconsistencies

- **"€[350–500]k"** — a 43% spread is not a fundable ask. Give a number with a contingency line.
- **"Estimable to ±[20]%"** — a blanket precision claim applied to niche premium segment sizing in a foreign market. It will not be ±20%. Either differentiate by item or drop the figure.
- **Audience confusion:** the header addresses "Board / Executive Committee." These want different documents and can approve different things (a board with outside investors changes what may be asked). Pick one.
- **"Month [30]"** for Korea is spuriously precise relative to everything around it; use a trigger condition ("Korea entry opens when Japan hits [X] repeat rate and [Y] wholesale doors"), which is also more consistent with the gate philosophy.
- **Gate numbering:** "Gate 0/1" in the header, Gate 0 = researched / Gate 1 = contracted in §0.1, kill criteria at §14.4 but gate sequence at §15. Tighten before the body is written or the cross-references will not survive.
- **Wrong-question table:** five rows with overlap between rows 1 and 3 (both are cost/consequence framings). Three sharper rows beat five.
- **Stylistic saturation:** three aphorisms of identical construction ("no claim travels faster than its evidence," "cannot be argued with... cannot be improved," "or they are guesses") in under two pages. The register begins to read as house style rather than analysis, which undercuts the empiricism being claimed.

---

## 8. What genuinely works and must be preserved

- **Separating demand entry from supply entry** is the correct central insight and is the document's real contribution. Most treatments of this brief conflate them.
- **Corollary 1 (landed-cost-after-risk)** is precise, correctly ordered, and immediately usable.
- **Corollary 2 ("most international expansion failure is domestic")** is the single most valuable sentence here — and should be promoted into a hard constraint with an attention budget attached, not left as an aphorism.
- **The three-tier confidence taxonomy** (verifiable fact / researchable quantity / design target) is a genuinely strong governance device and better than the single "[target]" convention it inherited.
- **Wholesale-first as buying market truth with someone else's working capital** is exactly right for a mid-sized brand's capital position.
- **"Rule of the document: every commitment has a stated cost to the core"** is a good discipline

# WHERE WE GROW NEXT
## International expansion: demand entry and supply entry as two separate decisions

**Board decision paper | v2.0**
*(The management committee counterpart, with vendor-level detail and the full research brief, is Annex 1 and is not required for this decision.)*

**Decision sought:** approval of the two-track structure, the beachhead selection method and its result, the positioning boundary, the channel sequence, the origin rule in §6.2, and **€290k (plus €45k contingency) to fund Gate 0**. Country choice becomes irrevocable only at Gate 1.

---

## The recommendation in one paragraph

Expansion into "a new region" is two decisions, not one. **Demand entry** and **supply entry** have different criteria, different clock speeds, different failure modes and different owners; fusing them into a single geography is how mid-sized brands lose margin in both. We propose a **Demand Track** entering **Japan** as beachhead — chosen on the scored criteria in §3.2, not asserted — with **South Korea opened by trigger, not by date** (§3.5); and a **Supply Track** qualifying **Vietnam** as a new manufacturing origin while retaining **Portugal and Turkey** as nearshore replenishment and **India as a source of certified organic fibre and yarn only**. The two tracks meet at one technical point and it is not the one an earlier draft claimed: preference eligibility is governed by **rules of origin, not by where the sewing happens**, which produces a single hard rule — **fibre and yarn may cross borders; fabric may not** (§6.2). Positioning is *not* "well-made sustainable basics"; Uniqlo and Muji own that ground in Japan permanently and will out-execute us on it forever. We enter as a **provable-longevity** brand — garments sold with their own evidence and their own repair — at a price architecture that never competes with either (§4). Channels are sequenced credibility-first and capital-last: distributor and wholesale before any entity, lease or local payroll, so that a failed entry costs a contract rather than a balance sheet (§5, §10.3). Two claims in this paper are load-bearing and are therefore **not** asserted: that Vietnamese vertical certified-organic fabric capacity exists at our quality and volume, and that Japan out-scores Korea on willingness-to-pay for provenance. Gate 0 exists to test exactly those two things, and §3.6 states in advance what result would flip the recommendation.
